analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare offer its own drug plan and negotiate prescription prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 51 House Democrats, was referred to two House committees and never received a vote, dying when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Medicare-run prescription drug plan available nationwide, and required Medicare to negotiate drug prices with manufacturers on behalf of people enrolled in it — breaking the rule, written into the 2003 Medicare drug law, that bars the government from negotiating. It would have automatically enrolled low-income subsidy recipients in the public plan, expanded help for low-income seniors, required plans to cover all drugs in six key categories (including benzodiazepines, which were excluded), barred plans from dropping drugs from their formularies mid-year, added criminal penalties for enrollment fraud, required faster payment of pharmacy claims, and eliminated a Medicare Advantage stabilization fund and certain Medicare Advantage overpayments.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — especially the roughly 25 million seniors and disabled people in Part D, dual eligibles, and low-income subsidy recipients — would benefit from lower negotiated prices, a uniform national premium, a public plan option, stronger formulary and appeal protections, and expanded low-income help. Retail pharmacies would benefit from prompt-payment rules and paid medication-therapy-management services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries, low-income seniors, and pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans with a nationwide service area and to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered Part D drugs, overriding the existing statutory bar on such negotiation.
Provides for auto-enrollment of subsidy-eligible individuals in the Medicare-operated plan, with notice of their right to choose another plan instead.

Requires that the monthly premium for the Medicare-operated plan be uniform nationally, based on average per-capita cost certified by the chief actuary of CMS, and allows negotiated savings to be applied to shrinking the coverage gap.

Expands low-income protections: raises the asset limits for full low-income subsidies, exempts life insurance and pension balances from resource counts, eliminates Part D cost-sharing for many non-institutionalized dual eligibles, waives late-enrollment penalties for subsidy-eligible people, and allows a one-time plan change during the first year of enrollment.

Bars prescription drug plans from removing a covered drug from the formulary, downgrading its cost-sharing tier, or adding barriers like prior authorization or step therapy without advance notice, and requires formularies to cover all or substantially all drugs in six therapeutic categories (immunosuppressants, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, antiretrovirals, and antineoplastics) without utilization-management tools.

Adds a criminal penalty of 3 to 10 years imprisonment for defrauding individuals in connection with Medicare Advantage or drug plan enrollment, creates a complaint process for people enrolled without informed consent, requires prompt payment of clean pharmacy claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper) with interest penalties, and extends coverage to benzodiazepines and medication therapy management services.

Eliminates the Medicare Advantage Regional Stabilization Fund and certain Medicare Advantage overpayments, and makes public the price information that currently stays confidential between manufacturers and dispensers.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear lower prices through negotiation; Medicare Advantage insurers and private prescription drug plan sponsors would lose overpayments and a stabilization fund, face stricter formulary, prompt-payment, and fraud rules, and compete with a government-run plan; the federal government would absorb costs of expanded low-income subsidies and premium protections, partly offset by the eliminated overpayments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, Medicare Advantage insurers, and Part D plans

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Secretary discretion to spend the savings from negotiated prices on reducing the coverage gap only 'to the extent practicable', and the cost of expanded low-income subsidies, premium protections, and the government-run plan would fall on the federal budget unless fully offset by the eliminated Medicare Advantage overpayments.

A Medicare-operated plan with the power to negotiate would compete directly with private Part D plans, and the bill auto-enrolls subsidy-eligible individuals into it — a good-faith objection is that this could crowd private plans out of large parts of the market, a structure critics of the 2003 law's public-option debates warned about.

Requiring formularies to cover all drugs in six categories without prior authorization or step therapy could raise premiums and plan costs, since plans would lose tools to steer utilization toward cheaper equivalents, though the bill encourages use of affordable therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections and low-income expansions are concrete and directly relieve seniors' costs. The core benefit — government negotiation — depends on how aggressively the Secretary negotiates, since the bill directs negotiation without setting price targets. The main real costs are budgetary (expanded subsidies, partly offset by eliminating Medicare Advantage overpayments) and the competitive disruption to private Part D plans, which the bill's authors would call a feature and its critics a flaw. On balance the bill's benefits to beneficiaries are large relative to its acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2007, referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on July 12, 2007, with 43 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred on the day of introduction to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means.
The only subsequent action was referral to the Subcommittee on Health on July 20, 2007; no committee report, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
By the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009, the bill had gathered 50 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died without any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the statutory bar on Medicare price negotiation, and Medicare Advantage insurers and private Part D plans kept the existing payment and market structure with no public-plan competitor. Seniors and taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 12, 2007 and promoted a Medicare-run drug plan with direct price negotiation.

for.name: 50 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 51 House members.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Health subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or floor vote during the remainder of the 110th Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA and member companies)
against.what_they_did: Opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices and defended the non-interference provision the bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; no Republican ever acted on the bill and no floor vote occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare to negotiate purchase prices for Part D drugs, ending the arrangement in which the government is barred from negotiating and pays manufacturers' list-based prices. Lower negotiated prices would mean lower drug costs for seniors and lower federal reimbursements for the industry.

The bill eliminates the Medicare Advantage Regional Stabilization Fund and extends certain overpayments' phase-out beyond 2010, cutting federal payments the industry currently receives. Those overpayments cost taxpayers and are not passed to beneficiaries under this bill.

industries.industry: Private Part D prescription drug plan sponsors (insurers and PBMs)
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan with negotiated prices, plus auto-enrollment of subsidy-eligible individuals into it, would take premium revenue and enrolled lives away from private plans. The bill also imposes stricter formulary, prompt-payment, and anti-fraud rules on them.

The bill requires plans to pay clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper) with interest for delay, requires plans to network enough retail pharmacies for medication therapy management, and pays pharmacists based on time and intensity of those services. It also bars pharmacy co-branding on drug plan cards.
